summary: The Sound recorder keeps the microphone's samples while it records, shows them as a waveform and a spectrogram, trims them and saves them. The WAV file it writes reads back sample for sample, and the browser decodes it to the same samples.

claims.claim: Save as WAV keeps every recorded sample (16-bit PCM, mono, at the microphone's rate).
claims.how: A standard RIFF WAVE header and 16-bit little-endian samples.

sources.title: WAV
sources.says: WAV is a container for, among others, LPCM: uncompressed linear pulse-code modulation.

claims.note: The in-page test records a 1 kHz tone from a fake microphone, trims it to 0.5 s, writes the file, reads it back and decodes it with the browser: within half a step of 16 bits.

claims.claim: The spectrogram shows which pitches the recording holds over time, 40 Hz to 16 kHz.
claims.how: The song landscape's short-time Fourier transform (studio-audio.js), 200 slices, 12 bands an octave.

sources.title: Spectrogram
sources.says: A spectrogram shows a signal's spectrum as it varies with time, computed from the short-time Fourier transform of windowed slices.

claims.claim: Trim the silence keeps the span louder than 40 dB below the loudest 20 ms.
claims.how: Levels of 20 ms slices; the first and last above the threshold, with one slice of margin.
claims.note: A rule of the toy, not a standard.

simplified: Each trim's ends fade over 5 ms so the cut doesn't click.
The smaller file is the browser's own Opus or AAC encoding of the trimmed sound, made in real time; it is lossy.
